This document is a summary of the first nine pages of the Constitution of the United States. Its main points are: [1] The U.S. Constitution establishes a bicameral legislature with two houses: the House of Representatives, which has members elected every two years by popular vote; and the Senate, where Senators serve six-year terms chosen by state legislatures. [2] Both houses must have at least 50% of their members present to conduct business legally. Revenue-raising bills originate in the House of Representatives, requiring a two-thirds supermajority vote for certain actions like expelling a member or convicting someone in an impeachment trial. The Senate holds sole authority over impeachments, with judgments limited to removal from office and disqualification from future federal offices. [3] Bills passed by both houses must be presented to the President; if signed, they become law immediately, but if not returned within ten days (excluding Sundays), they automatically take effect unless Congress adjourns. If the President returns a bill with objections, it requires a two-thirds vote in each house to pass before becoming law. Congress holds powers including taxing and regulating commerce, establishing bankruptcy rules, maintaining a navy, raising armies (with state appointments), and appointing officers for the militia. [4] The Constitution was ratified by nine states on September 17, 1787. Article III defines treason as levying war against or aiding the enemies of the United States, with conviction limited to cases proven by two witnesses or a court confession. It declares federal laws and treaties as supreme law, requiring officers to swear an oath while prohibiting religious tests for office, and ensures all debts remain valid under this new framework. Summary of all 9 pages.
